newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria steps up fight against car theft.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria steps up fight against car theft.

text.p: Bulgaria has started confiscating luxury cars for checks, stepping up a fight against a huge trade in vehicles stolen abroad and against corruption, interim Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev said on Thursday.
"Today the interior ministry for the first time launched a raid codenamed Mosquito and started to 'arrest' luxury cars in order to check whether they are lawfully owned," Bonev said.

He said detained vehicles were checked for paid customs duties and taxes. Owners should also prove that they have bought their vehicles legally and the origin of the money they bought them with, Bonev told reporters.
The checks are expected to last up to a month. "Until then the cars will be detained," Bonev said.
Witnesses said policemen began to stop luxury cars in the streets and had escorted them to the interior ministry's armed forces barracks at Vranja at the outskirts of Sofia.
There were more than 500 vehicles parked in the yard, most of them new Mercedes, BMWs, Audis and jeeps, a witness, who declined to be named, told Reuters.
He said riot police had beaten people as they were waiting in their cars at the barracks' parking lot.
"Policemen with black hoods over their faces started beating us with truncheons or hands without saying a word. We ran away from the place," he said.
The ministry said in a statement it would probe into citizens' complaints of use of excessive force by some policemen.
It said it had returned seized cars to firms and banks.
Crime has soared since the collapse of communist rule in 1989. The police are poorly paid, ill-equipped and vulnerable to corruption.

Car thefts make up one fifth of all crime, officials say. Organised groups, working with gangs in Western Europe, alter the appearance of stolen cars, change licence plates, scrape off engine and car body numbers and engrave new ones to match forged documents.
Police say the traffic of stolen cars through Bulgaria is huge, many vehicles being re-exported to Moldova, Ukraine and other ex-Soviet republics or Macedonia, Albania, and Yugoslavia.
